Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Starting with the first turn, players will take alternating turns. Each turn, the active player chooses one of the two visible actions (not covered by the Rooster), on their action area: • Add an animal • Move an animal After performing the action, the Rooster must be moved on top of the symbol of the performed action, as an indicator that the player’s turn is over (automated on BGA). If a player no longer has animals left to add to the game board, they are no longer required to move the Rooster and, from then on, will always move an animal as their action. If a player still has animals to add and is forced to add an animal, but the rules don't allow the animal to be placed, the game ends and the other player wins. Contents 1 Placement rules 2 Add an animal 3 Move an animal 4 End of game Placement rules The Donkey can only be placed at ground level on an empty square. The Dog can only be placed on top of an already placed Donkey or at ground level on an empty square. The Cat can only be placed on top of an already placed Dog or at ground level on an empty square. Add an animal To add an animal, the player chooses one of their animals and places it on the game board by following the placement rules. Once an animal is added to the board, it will become available to any player. Move an animal To move an animal, the player chooses any animal or stack of animals from the ones already on the game board and moves it to any other space by following the placement rules. To move a stack of animals the player must always keep their stack order but can move a portion of a stack. A player cannot invert the last player’s action. End of game The aim of the game is to complete a line of three animals of the same type in either a horizontal, diagonal or vertical row. Only the top animal of each stack or animals standing alone will be considered to determine a complete line. The first player who places the third animal on a complete line of animals of the same type wins the game. [Rating: 1/10] Fast and simple. But I found that it's a game of watching your enemy slip and then go in for the kill. The game is just too tight to make clever moves, like, say, Tak - let alone classics like Chess, Go, Shogi

[Rating: 2/10] If it wasn't $30, I'd recommend this as a gift to children from 6-10. However it's like Boop in the sense that there isn't much depth to the whole game, and its a decision tree that's pretty easy to work out. For those who do not like complex games, this might be an enjoyable experience once. But I think it's a forgettable over-priced game.

[Rating: 3/10] A pretty simple abstract that did nothing to really diffentiate itself beside having fun minis in an oversized box.

[Rating: 4/10] Kinda like Tic Tac Toe meets Santorini, with 3 types of pieces (base, middle, top).  You're trying to get 3 in row of same type of piece.  You have 2 actions - to place a piece or move a stack of pieces (where you can choose to move only part of the stack).  You can move them anywhere, not just adjacent, but if moving to an occupied space you must be able to stack on top of the existing piece(s). [Rating: 4/10] This is a very nice product altough expensive: the box like a book, the miniatures, the concept based on the german fable "Die Bremer Stadtmusikanten". About the gameplay: pure abstract games do not entertain me.

[Rating: 5/10] Abstract based off of tic tac toe where you have no specific piece you are associated with to win and can stack some pieces in order to sort of remove the bottom piece from consideration for winning. A fine design, I have just grown a little tired of this type of abstract game.

[Rating: 5/10] Seems like a perfectly fine pure abstract of a sort I just don't particularly care for.

[Rating: 5/10] Found on BGA - 2p abstract game to get 3 in a row with various pieces. Definitely an easy-to-learn game and works well for fans of abstract games. It is a small 3x3 grid so you have to be on your toes to block your opponent. It is fine but doesn't really stand out for me.
